stages.title: Advanced linguistics and grammar
stages.hook: Why do Greek speakers use two past tenses, έγραφα and έγραψα? What does the difference show about how Greek views an action?
explain: Greek verbs have two stems for aspect: an imperfective stem for ongoing or repeated actions (γράφ-) and a perfective stem for a complete event (γράψ-). So έγραφα (imperfect) says "I was writing, I used to write", while έγραψα (aorist) says "I wrote, I finished". In the future θα γράφω is continuous or repeated and θα γράψω is a single act.

Modern Greek has lost the infinitive. Instead of an infinitive, it uses να plus a finite verb, a feature shared with other Balkan languages. It also has clitic pronouns and "clitic doubling": Το βιβλίο το διάβασα (the book, I read it). Nouns and adjectives inflect for case, gender and number, which makes Greek a fusional language.
stages.mnemonic: Two stems, two cameras: one filming the process, one taking a snapshot.
sentences: The aorist shows a completed action.
The case shows the relation of the word.

gq.q: What does έγραψα express compared with έγραφα?
gq.why: The aorist views the action as a whole.

gq.q: How does Modern Greek replace the infinitive?
o: With να plus a finite verb
gq.why: The infinitive disappeared during the history of Greek.

panel.q: Which feature does Greek share with other Balkan languages?
panel.why: Balkan Sprachbund languages replaced the infinitive with finite clauses.

panel.q: What is clitic doubling in Το βιβλίο το διάβασα?
o: The object is both named and repeated by a weak pronoun
panel.why: The pronoun το echoes the object το βιβλίο.

panel.q: Why is θα γράφω different from θα γράψω?
o: The first views the future action as ongoing or repeated, the second as a single event
panel.why: Aspect appears in all tenses.

teach.model: Greek has an imperfective stem and a perfective stem. Έγραφα is ongoing, έγραψα is complete. Greek has no infinitive and uses να plus a finite verb. It also uses clitic pronouns.

trip.prompt: Read about aspect and find two verbs with both stems.

stages.title: Historical development of the language
stages.hook: Greek has been written for over 3,000 years. What do we know about its oldest written form?
explain: Greek forms its own branch of the Indo-European family. The oldest deciphered writing is Linear B, used for Mycenaean Greek around the second millennium BCE; Michael Ventris deciphered it in 1952. The later alphabet came from the Phoenician script, and the Greeks added signs for vowels.

Stages of the language are Ancient Greek (including Attic of classical Athens), Koine (the common Greek of the Hellenistic period and the New Testament), Byzantine or Medieval Greek, and Modern Greek. Alexandrian scholars created accents and breathing marks. In the 20th century the "language question" between formal καθαρεύουσα and spoken δημοτική ended in 1976 in favour of demotic.
stages.mnemonic: Linear B, alphabet, Koine, Byzantine, Modern: a long road with one language.
sentences: Koine was the language of the Hellenistic period.
The alphabet comes from the Phoenician.

gq.why: Ventris showed that Linear B writes an early form of Greek.

gq.q: What did the Greeks add to the Phoenician script?
gq.why: The Phoenician script wrote consonants, and Greek adapted some signs for vowels.

panel.q: Why is Koine important?
o: It was the language of Athens only
It was the common Greek of the Hellenistic world and of the New Testament
panel.why: Koine spread across the Eastern Mediterranean.

panel.q: What was the "language question"?
o: A debate about the Latin script
The debate over formal καθαρεύουσα versus spoken δημοτική
panel.why: It ended in 1976 when demotic became official.

panel.q: Why do Greek words appear in many European languages?
o: Greek was a source of scientific, philosophical and cultural vocabulary
Greek is the root of all languages
panel.why: Greek roots are widely used in terminology.

teach.model: Greek is its own branch of Indo-European. Linear B, deciphered in 1952, is the oldest. Ancient Greek, Koine, Byzantine Greek and Modern Greek are its stages. The Greek alphabet came from the Phoenician and added vowels.

trip.prompt: Find the timeline and list the main stages in order.

stages.title: Literature and cultural discourse
stages.hook: Greek songs that no one wrote down have lasted for centuries. How?
explain: Modern Greek literature has deep roots in oral tradition. The δημοτικό τραγούδι (folk song) kept stories of heroes, love and exile alive for generations. The Modern Greek Enlightenment and the 1821 Revolution shaped writing in the 19th century.

The Generation of the '30s (η γενιά του τριάντα) renewed poetry and prose and included Giorgos Seferis and Odysseas Elytis. Both won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Greek diaspora (διασπορά), communities in many countries, became part of Greek identity, and writers often explore memory, exile and the dialogue between ancient heritage and modern life.
stages.mnemonic: Songs travel on voices, books travel on paper, and both carry Greece.
sentences: The Generation of the '30s renewed poetry.
The folk song keeps the tradition.
The diaspora became part of the identity.

gq.q: Which poets belong to the Generation of the '30s?
gq.why: Seferis and Elytis are central figures.

o: A folk song from oral tradition
gq.why: Demotic songs preserved stories and values.

panel.q: Why is oral tradition important to Greek literature?
o: It was invented in the 20th century
It preserved stories and a poetic language before and beyond print
panel.why: Folk songs influenced later poets.

panel.q: What can the diaspora contribute to a national culture?
o: New experiences, memory and exchange with other cultures
panel.why: Diaspora writing adds perspectives on identity.

panel.q: Why do writers revisit ancient heritage?
o: It offers shared images and a way to reflect on modern life
panel.why: Dialogue with the past is a recurring theme.

teach.model: Greek literature draws on oral folk songs and on the Generation of the '30s, including Seferis and Elytis, both Nobel laureates. The diaspora is part of Greek identity.

trip.prompt: Read the section on poetry and note two writers.

stages.title: Advanced academic writing
stages.hook: Academic Greek builds long chains of genitives. What does "Σκοπός της εργασίας" tell the reader?
explain: A Greek academic text opens with a περίληψη (abstract), then gives the σκοπός (aim), the ερευνητικό ερώτημα (research question), the μεθοδολογία (methodology) and the συμπεράσματα (conclusions). A βιβλιογραφία lists sources, and παραπομπές (citations) or υποσημειώσεις (footnotes) credit them.

Style is impersonal and precise: Σκοπός της εργασίας είναι η ανάλυση των δεδομένων. Genitive chains such as η ανάλυση των δεδομένων are typical. Hedges mark caution: φαίνεται ότι (it seems that), ενδεχομένως (possibly), πιθανώς (probably). Avoid colloquial words and ensure consistent accents and terminology.
stages.mnemonic: Abstract, aim, question, method, conclusion: a map of a paper.
sentences: The aim of the work is the analysis of the data.
The methodology is described in section two.
The citations are listed at the end.

panel.q: Why is the style impersonal?
o: It focuses attention on method and results
It is required by the alphabet
panel.why: Impersonal style is standard in research.

panel.q: What role does a research question play?
o: It guides the whole study and defines what to find out
panel.why: A clear question gives direction.

panel.q: Why must citations be consistent?
o: Readers must be able to locate every source
panel.why: Consistent form supports verification.

teach.model: A Greek academic text has a περίληψη, σκοπός, ερευνητικό ερώτημα, μεθοδολογία, συμπεράσματα and βιβλιογραφία. The style is impersonal, with genitive chains and hedges like φαίνεται ότι.

trip.prompt: Read the page on academic structure and sketch an outline of a short paper.

stages.title: Professional translation
stages.hook: A Greek sign says "Απαγορεύεται το κάπνισμα". How should a translator render the style?
explain: Professional translation aims for the same effect on the target reader. Greek signs use "Απαγορεύεται το κάπνισμα" (literally "Smoking is forbidden"), while English uses "No smoking". A word-for-word version would sound odd, so the translator uses a translation shift (μεταφραστική μετατόπιση).

Professionals use a glossary (γλωσσάρι) for consistency, check collocations, localise units, dates and conventions (τοπική προσαρμογή) and finish with proofreading (διόρθωση). Names are transliterated by a stated system, such as ELOT 743, which matches ISO 843, so spellings may differ between sources. Pragmatics (πραγματολογία) matters: the text must function as the original does.
sentences: The translator must know the terminology.

gq.q: How is Απαγορεύεται το κάπνισμα best rendered on an English sign?
gq.why: Translators follow the conventional form of the target language.

o: To keep terms consistent across a text
gq.why: Consistency is a mark of quality.

panel.q: Why can Greek names have several Latin spellings?
panel.why: Systems differ in handling letters such as χ or υ.

panel.q: What is the aim of localisation?
o: To adapt a text to the target culture, including units and dates
panel.why: Localisation goes beyond translating words.

panel.q: What is a common shift when translating from Greek to English?
o: Impersonal passive forms turned into active or noun forms
panel.why: English often prefers a different structure.

teach.model: A professional translator aims for the same effect on the reader. Use glossaries for consistency, conventional forms like No smoking for Απαγορεύεται το κάπνισμα, localisation and proofreading.

points.ask: What is the aim of translation?
How do I keep terms consistent?

trip.prompt: Read about translation shifts and write one Greek-English example.

stages.title: Interpretation of complex communication
stages.hook: Someone says "Κάνει κρύο εδώ" and looks at the window. What do they probably want?
explain: Interpreting complex communication means reading beyond the words. Κάνει κρύο εδώ (It is cold here) may be an indirect request to close the window. Implied meaning (υπονοούμενο), hints (νύξεις), irony (ειρωνεία), euphemism (ευφημισμός) and figurative use (μεταφορική χρήση) all need context, intonation and shared knowledge.

Polysemy (πολυσημία) means that one word has several senses, and context selects the sense. Irony is often shown by intonation: Μπράβο σου! said after a mistake means the opposite of praise. Euphemisms soften sensitive facts: Έφυγε από τη ζωή for "died". Non-verbal signals (μη λεκτική επικοινωνία), such as an upward head tilt meaning "no", also carry meaning.
stages.mnemonic: The words say one thing; the situation says another.
sentences: Irony is seen in the intonation.

gq.q: A friend breaks your cup and you say "Μπράβο σου!" with a sharp tone. What do you convey?
o: A request for a new cup

gq.q: What is Έφυγε από τη ζωή?
gq.why: It is a softer way to say died.

panel.q: What does Κάνει κρύο εδώ often communicate?
o: An indirect request, such as closing the window
panel.why: Pragmatic meaning goes beyond the literal.

panel.q: Why does an interpreter need cultural knowledge?
o: Meaning often depends on shared background, not just words
panel.why: Cultural context decides implied meaning.

panel.q: How does polysemy create difficulty?
o: One word may have several senses, so context must select the right one
panel.why: The interpreter chooses the sense from context.

teach.model: Meaning can go beyond words: implication, hints, irony, euphemism and indirect requests. Use context, intonation and cultural knowledge. Polysemy means that one word has several senses.

trip.prompt: Read about implicature and find an example of an indirect request.

stages.title: Language variation and dialectology
stages.hook: Is there one single Greek, or many varieties? Linguists study this question.
explain: Dialectology studies regional varieties (διάλεκτοι, ιδιώματα). Standard Modern Greek (κοινή νεοελληνική) is based on the demotic language. Greek dialects include Pontic (ποντιακά), Cypriot (κυπριακά), Cretan (κρητικά) and Tsakonian (τσακώνικα), the only surviving descendant of ancient Doric, spoken in a small area of the Peloponnese.

Northern Greek dialects typically drop or raise unstressed vowels, so that words can sound different from the southern or standard pronunciation. Social varieties exist too, such as slang and professional jargon. Speakers move between standard and local speech according to situation, and language contact shapes variation in the diaspora.
sentences: The Cypriot dialect has special sounds.
Standard Modern Greek is based on demotic.

o: A Greek variety descended from Doric
gq.why: It is the only surviving descendant of Doric.

gq.q: What is Standard Modern Greek based on?

panel.q: Why do speakers switch between varieties?
o: Different situations call for different registers
panel.why: Style shifting is normal.

panel.q: What do northern dialects often do with unstressed vowels?
panel.why: Vowel raising and deletion are typical of northern varieties.

panel.q: Why do dialect speakers in the diaspora keep or change their speech?
o: Contact and community identity shape it
panel.why: Language contact and identity influence use.

teach.model: Dialectology studies regional and social varieties. Standard Modern Greek is based on demotic. Greek varieties include Pontic, Cypriot, Cretan and Tsakonian, a descendant of Doric.

points.ask: What is the standard based on?

trip.prompt: Find a map of Greek dialects and name three.

stages.title: Specialised scientific or technical language
stages.hook: The word "biology" is Greek. Can you split it into its two Greek parts?
explain: Scientific vocabulary is full of Greek roots: βιολογία comes from βίος (life) and λόγος (study), and τηλεσκόπιο from τηλε- (far) and σκοπώ (I look). International terms such as εξίσωση (equation), αλγόριθμος (algorithm), μόριο (molecule), πείραμα (experiment), σφάλμα (error), τύπος (formula) and ταχύτητα (speed) form the base of technical Greek.

Technical texts are impersonal and precise: Το πείραμα επιβεβαίωσε τον τύπο. Prefixes such as υπερ-, υπο- and μετα- and suffixes such as -λογία and -μετρία form new terms. Numbers use a decimal comma: 3,5. Clarity and exact terminology matter more than style.
stages.mnemonic: Bios plus logos: life plus study.
sentences: The speed of light is constant.

gq.q: What are the two roots of βιολογία?
gq.why: Βίος is life and λόγος is study or word.
Greek uses a comma as the decimal separator.

panel.q: Why does a Greek speaker recognise many scientific terms easily?
o: Many are built from familiar Greek roots
panel.why: Roots like -λογία and τηλε- are part of ordinary Greek.

panel.q: Why must scientific language be unambiguous?
o: Results need to be reproduced and understood exactly
panel.why: Precision supports reproducibility.

panel.q: What does the prefix υπερ- usually mean?
panel.why: For example υπερήχοι are ultrasounds.

teach.model: Scientific Greek is precise and uses roots like βίος and λόγος. Prefixes and suffixes form new terms. Texts are impersonal and numbers use a decimal comma.

trip.prompt: Find three Greek roots and the English words that contain them.

stages.title: Integrated proficiency project
stages.hook: You must present a small research project in Greek. Which steps bring all your language knowledge together?
explain: An integrated project combines reading, research, writing and speaking. Choose a topic, collect sources, state the aim and the κύριο αποτέλεσμα (main result), explain the περιορισμοί (limitations) and give a σύσταση (recommendation). Support claims with τεκμήρια (evidence) and acknowledge other views.

In the final presentation use signposts (Συνοψίζοντας, Προτείνω να εξετάσουμε...), a clear structure, accurate cases and aspect, correct accents and a suitable register. Be ready for questions: Επιτρέψτε μου να διευκρινίσω... (Allow me to clarify...). Peer review (αξιολόγηση από ομότιμους) improves quality: invite comments and revise.
stages.mnemonic: Topic, evidence, result, limits, recommendation: a project in five steps.
sentences: The main result is confirmed by the data.
The limitations of the study are described below.
I propose that we examine another approach.

gq.q: Which phrase politely asks to clarify?
Why state the limitations of a study?
o: To show honestly how far the conclusions can be trusted

panel.q: What does peer review contribute?
o: Independent feedback that improves accuracy and clarity
panel.why: Review catches errors and gaps.

panel.q: Which order best fits a project report?
panel.why: The logical flow helps the reader.

panel.q: A listener challenges your claim. What is a good response?
o: Give evidence and acknowledge valid doubts
panel.why: Argument rests on evidence and openness.

teach.model: A project combines reading, research, writing and speaking. State the aim, main result, limitations and recommendation, support claims with evidence and use a suitable register. Invite peer review.

points.ask: How do I improve my project?

trip.prompt: Read about the research process and list its steps.
